title: Skull Nebula NGC 246
caption: The Skull Nebula, NGC 246, imaged by the Gemini South telescope

recognition.text: Official NSF NOIRLab / Gemini press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: This Gemini South image shows NGC 246, a planetary nebula in the constellation Cetus, nicknamed the Skull Nebula in the image's title. It lies about 1,600 light-years away.

Despite the name, planetary nebulae have nothing to do with planets. They are shells of gas thrown off by stars like the Sun near the end of their lives, lit up by the hot, exposed core left behind at the centre. Over time the shell spreads out and fades into space, while the core slowly cools.

The central star of NGC 246 shines at 12th magnitude, far too faint to see without a telescope. It is also moving quickly, whisking through space at about 80 kilometres (50 miles) per second. The image was made with the Gemini Multi-Object Spectrograph through filters for sulfur, hydrogen-alpha and oxygen, which each capture the glow of a different gas in the shell.
scale: NGC 246 lies about 1,600 light-years away, according to the International Gemini Observatory.

understand.summary: Taken in visible light with GMOS on Gemini South through S II, hydrogen-alpha and [O III] filters. The colour mapping isn't published.
understand.eye: Narrow filters isolate the glow of particular gases, and the long exposure gathers far more light than the eye could.
